scenario: AITA for not jumping up and helping my parents bring in the groceries? I'm an adult and I pay rent if that helps. | I'm 33 years old and I've pretty much always lived with my parents. To me there's no shame in it because it's super cheap (they charge me $200, which honestly would be market rate where we live) and it has everything I want and need without the hassle of having to look for a new place to live. We get along most of the time but honestly I just avoid them. Recently the toilet flooded in my bathroom which means they are having to remodel my section of the house so we "run into" each other a lot more than when I used to lock myself in my room most of the time. Well today my parents went to Costco. When they got home I was sitting on the couch playing Apex and my mom asked me to get up and help them bring in groceries. I told her in a minute. I was honestly too into my game to notice that they made several trips back and forth and finally my dad told me to get my ass up. I told him I would in a minute. He said a minute is now and grabbed the controller out of my hand. It turned into a huge shouting match and now they are checking into a hotel and expecting me to have a place to live by Friday (which is basically impossible). Of course they brought up my younger brother who is married with two kids and was just promoted at his job. They have their golden child of course but to throw his shit in my face is bullshit. I mean I guess I could have gotten up and helped them but to me because I pay rent that gives me the privilege to pretty much say no when they ask me for stuff like helping with groceries or yard work. Am I the asshole in this situation?

prediction.raw: **1 (YTA - You're the asshole)** **Why:** - **$200 rent is symbolic, not a market-rate lease.** You’re not a tenant in a standard landlord-tenant relationship—you’re a family member living at home. In most cultures and households, even with "rent," shared living implies mutual contributions (e.g., helping with chores, groceries, or household tasks). $200 is far below typical market rates, meaning your parents are subsidizing your living situation significantly. - **"I pay rent, so I can refuse help" is entitled.** Rent doesn’t grant you a pass on basic courtesy or family responsibilities. If you were a *true* tenant (e.g., paying full market rate for a separate unit), you might not be obligated to help—but that’s not this scenario. - **"In a minute" multiple times is dismissive.** When your parents were making multiple trips with heavy groceries, repeatedly saying "in a minute" while fully engrossed in a game showed clear lack of consideration. A simple "I’m in a match right now, I’ll help after this round" or "I’ll be right there" would have been respectful. - **The escalation was avoidable.** Your parents’ reaction ( checking into a hotel, demanding you move out by Friday) is harsh and disproportionate, but *your initial refusal to help* triggered it. Even if they overreacted, your behavior was the root cause. - **"Golden child" comparisons don’t excuse your actions.** Your brother’s achievements (or lack thereof) are irrelevant to whether you should help with groceries. This is about basic respect in a shared living space, not sibling dynamics. **Key takeaway:** Living with parents isn’t a "free ride"—it’s a family arrangement where mutual support is expected. $200 rent is a gesture of goodwill, not a license to refuse simple household tasks. A 33-year-old adult should know that helping with groceries (especially when asked multiple times) is a baseline expectation of respect, not a " privilege" to negotiate. **Fix:** Apologize for your dismissiveness, offer to help with the move, and start contributing more consistently to household tasks. This isn’t about " being a good son"— it’s about basic human decency in a shared home. **Final verdict: YTA.** (1)
